passage:
Thursday, 9:50 pm. Wasim bhai knocked on my door for the third time and asked, "Noor, what happened at school? You barely ate." I stayed on the bed and said nothing. My throat felt like a stone. Something happened with Sana and the group, and I cannot say it aloud yet without crying.
He sat on the floor by the door and did not push. "Okay. I'm not going to make you. But whenever you want to talk, tonight or next week or never, I'm here. No conditions, no questions first."
I said nothing again. But I did not feel alone. I might tell him on Sunday.
— Noor

qa.q: How many times did Wasim bhai knock on the door?
qa.a: Wasim bhai knocked for the third time.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling while staying silent on the bed?
qa.a: Noor felt hurt and unable to say it without crying, with a throat like a stone. The silence protects something painful, not rudeness.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that made Noor feel less alone?
qa.a: Wasim bhai sat on the floor, did not push and said Noor could talk whenever, with no conditions. That gave Noor room to decide.

qa.q: How might Wasim bhai have felt when Noor did not answer?
qa.a: Wasim bhai was probably worried but patient, since he did not press and stayed by the door. Offering to listen later showed care without demand.

grounding: A teenager who says nothing when questioned defends privacy and hides hurt, and is met with an offer to talk later with no conditions.

passage:
"Pranav, you've been silent since your mother asked about school. Let your Sarika Bua tell you something.
"At fifteen, I stopped talking at home. My best friend had turned the whole class against me, and I felt so ashamed I couldn't say it out loud. Every evening my mother asked, 'What's wrong? Tell me! Why are you like this?' The more she asked, the tighter my mouth closed.
"My father did something different. One night he knocked on my door and said, 'I won't ask what happened. But I'll be on the terrace every night after dinner. If you ever want to talk, come. No questions unless you want them.'
"I didn't go for a week. Then I went. We looked at the stars for twenty minutes. Then I told him everything.
"So, Pranav, I won't ask. But I'm around all week.

qa.q: Where did Sarika Bua's father say he'd be every night?
qa.a: He said he'd be on the terrace every night after dinner.

qa.q: Why did young Sarika go silent at home?
qa.a: Young Sarika felt deeply hurt and ashamed after her best friend turned the class against her, and couldn't say it aloud.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Her father stopped pressing and offered to be on the terrace with no questions, which gave her space and a safe door to open when ready.

qa.q: How did Sarika's mother likely feel during those weeks?
qa.a: Her mother was likely worried and frustrated, pressing harder because she couldn't bear not knowing what was wrong.

grounding: An elder recalls going silent as a teen to hide hurt, and how an offer to talk later with no conditions worked better than pressing.

passage:
The cousin's wedding in Kochi was loud with nadaswaram and chatter, and Gopika, fifteen, sat in a corner of the hall, not eating, not talking. Earlier, an aunt had said loudly, "Gopika has put on weight, na?" and people had laughed.
Her cousin Aadhya, twenty, found her. "Gopu, what's wrong?"
Gopika shrugged.
"Did someone say something? Tell me."
Nothing. Gopika stared at her plate, jaw tight.
Aadhya felt the urge to keep asking. The music was blaring; relatives kept interrupting to say hello. It was no place to talk.
She sat down beside Gopika instead. "Okay. I won't push. After the reception, I'm going to the beach with a cold coffee. If you want to come, come. We don't have to talk."
Gopika didn't answer.
But at nine, she was standing by the car, holding two coffees.

qa.q: What time was Gopika standing by the car?
qa.a: At nine, she was standing by the car, holding two coffees.

qa.q: Why did Gopika stay silent when Aadhya asked what was wrong?
qa.a: Gopika felt hurt and humiliated by the aunt's comment in front of everyone, and too ashamed to talk in the loud, crowded hall.

qa.q: Which of Aadhya's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya stopped pressing and offered a later, quiet time with no conditions, which let Gopika come when she was ready.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have felt when she saw Gopika by the car?
qa.a: Aadhya likely felt relieved and touched that Gopika had chosen to come, even bringing coffee for both of them.

grounding: A teenager stays silent to hide hurt, and an offer to talk later with no conditions works better than pressing.

passage:
In their Mumbai flat, Pallavi came home from school, dropped her bag and went straight to her room. At dinner, Irawati asked, "How was the class test?" Pallavi shrugged. "Did something happen with your friends?" Silence. "Pallavi, answer me when I talk to you."
Pallavi pushed her rice around, eyes down.
Irawati felt her worry turning into frustration. She opened her mouth to demand an answer, then remembered her own mother doing just that, and how it had made her lock her door.
She took a breath. "Okay. You don't have to tell me now. I'm going for a walk after dinner, around the colony. If you want to come, you can. If you want to talk, we'll talk. If not, we'll just walk."
Pallavi said nothing.
But when Irawati tied her shoes, Pallavi was at the door, hoodie on.
Halfway round the colony, she said, "Riya said something really mean today."

qa.q: Where was Irawati going after dinner?
qa.a: Irawati was going for a walk around the colony.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when Pallavi kept silent?
qa.a: Irawati felt worried, and the worry was turning into frustration as her questions got no answer.

qa.q: What worked better than demanding an answer, and why?
qa.a: Offering a walk with no conditions gave Pallavi space and privacy, so she chose to speak when she felt ready.

qa.q: Why might Pallavi have stayed silent at dinner?
qa.a: Pallavi was likely hurt by what Riya said and wasn't ready to talk under direct questions at the table.

grounding: A teenager's silence hides hurt, and an offer to talk later with no conditions works better than pressing harder.

passage:
"Zeenat, you tore up your own project. Three weeks of work. Why?"
Silence.
"Did someone say something? Was it the marks?"
She stared at the floor tiles.
"I'm asking you a question. Look at me."
Nothing. Her jaw set harder.
Shankar sir leaned back and let out a breath. "Okay. I'm pushing, and it isn't helping." He slid the torn pieces into a folder. "You don't owe me an answer today. I'm in the art room every day after lunch. If you want to talk, or just sit and draw, the door's open. No questions unless you want them."
Zeenat looked up for a second, then left.
Two days later, after lunch, she stood in the art room doorway. "It didn't look like it did in my head," she said quietly. "I worked so long, and it looked stupid."
"That feeling is awful," Shankar sir said. "Want to show me what was in your head?"
She pulled up a stool.

qa.q: How long had Zeenat worked on the project?
qa.a: Three weeks of work.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been feeling behind her set jaw and silence?
qa.a: She seems to have felt hurt and ashamed about the project and did not want to be pushed into explaining before she was ready.

qa.q: Which offer brought Zeenat back, and why?
qa.a: An open door in the art room after lunch with no conditions, talk or just draw, which let her choose her own time.

qa.q: Why might Shankar sir have stopped pressing?
qa.a: He noticed his questions were making Zeenat shut down harder, and he cared more about her talking eventually than answering right then.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stays silent under questioning to protect a hurt, and who comes to talk once the teacher stops pressing and offers a later chat with no conditions.
